examination: Gait and posture; observe antalgic gait, foot drop and heel/toe walking where safe.
Lumbar range of motion; note reproduction/peripheralization of leg symptoms.
Straight Leg Raise (SLR/Lasegue): reproduce concordant radicular pain; document angle and side.
Crossed SLR: reproduction of symptomatic-leg pain when the opposite leg is raised.
Slump test where appropriate as an additional neurodynamic test.
Motor: hip flexion (L2-3), knee extension (L3-4), ankle dorsiflexion (L4-5), great-toe extension (L5), plantar flexion (S1).
Sensory mapping: L4 medial leg/ankle, L5 dorsum foot/great toe tendency, S1 lateral foot/sole tendency.
Reflexes: patellar L3-4 and Achilles S1; compare sides.
Screen hip/SI joint and peripheral pulses if the pattern is atypical or vascular/hip disease is possible.
Always document bladder/bowel/saddle symptoms and progressive motor deficit.

investigations.indication: Uncomplicated acute low-back pain/sciatica without red flags; imaging rarely changes initial management.

investigations.test: X-ray Lumbosacral Spine — AP & Lateral views
investigations.indication: Consider when fracture/structural bony pathology is plausible: significant or low-velocity trauma with osteoporosis/older age, chronic steroid exposure, or selected persistent structural symptoms. Not a routine sciatica test.
Persistent/progressive radicular symptoms when intervention/surgery is being considered, or objective neurological deficit; correlate level and side with examination.
Suspected cauda equina syndrome or rapidly progressive major neurological deficit.
Only when infection/systemic inflammatory pathology is suspected.

medications.dose: 400 mg orally up to three times daily with/after food; use the lowest effective dose.
medications.duration: Shortest appropriate course; reassess early (typically within days, not an open-ended prescription).
medications.notes: NSAID option, not disease-modifying. Avoid/modify for peptic ulcer or GI bleed risk, CKD/AKI, significant cardiovascular risk, anticoagulants, NSAID hypersensitivity and pregnancy-related contraindications. Do not combine with another NSAID.

brandExamples: Voveran 50 GE / Voveran-D (diclofenac 50 mg; India-market examples)
medications.dose: Typical adult oral total 75–150 mg/day in divided doses; e.g. 50 mg twice daily, only if clinically appropriate.
medications.duration: Lowest effective dose for the shortest period; early reassessment.
medications.notes: Alternative NSAID, NOT together with ibuprofen/naproxen. Consider GI, renal, hepatic and cardiovascular risk and gastroprotection where indicated.

nonDrug: Explain favorable natural history where appropriate and encourage normal activity within tolerance; avoid prolonged bed rest.
Individualized exercise/rehabilitation based on irritability, neurological deficit and function.
Manual therapy, if used, should be part of an exercise-based package rather than stand-alone care.
Acute severe sciatica: image-guided/specialist epidural local anaesthetic + corticosteroid can be considered in selected patients.
Do NOT routinely use gabapentinoids/other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for sciatica; avoid chronic opioids.
followUp: Reassess pain distribution, SLR, motor power, sensory deficit, reflexes and gait.
Immediate escalation for new bladder/bowel/saddle symptoms or progressive motor weakness.
If disabling symptoms persist despite appropriate conservative care, obtain concordant imaging and consider spine specialist referral.

examination: Observe posture, gait and functional transitions (sit-to-stand, bending, walking).
Lumbar flexion, extension and side-bending; document painful/restricted patterns.
Palpation is supportive only; do not diagnose a pain generator from tenderness alone.
Neurological screen: motor, dermatomes, patellar/Achilles reflexes.
SLR if leg symptoms are present to screen radiculopathy.
Hip examination and SI screening when history suggests a non-lumbar source.
Red-flag screen: trauma, cancer, infection, inflammatory disease and cauda equina symptoms.

investigations.indication: Acute or subacute non-specific/mechanical low-back pain without red flags.

investigations.test: X-ray Lumbosacral Spine — AP & Lateral views
investigations.indication: Low-velocity/significant trauma, osteoporosis, older age, chronic steroid use, suspected compression fracture or selected structural concern.
Persistent/progressive symptoms after an adequate conservative trial when intervention is being considered, or new objective neurological findings.
Only when cancer, infection, inflammatory disease or postoperative complication is suspected.

medications.dose: 400 mg orally up to three times daily with/after food when an NSAID is appropriate.
medications.duration: Lowest effective dose for the shortest period; reassess within days.
medications.notes: Assess GI, renal, cardiovascular, allergy, anticoagulant and pregnancy risks; do not combine NSAIDs.

medications.dose: 75–150 mg/day in divided doses; commonly 50 mg twice daily when selected.
medications.notes: Alternative NSAID. Consider gastroprotection based on risk. Avoid duplicate NSAID therapy.

nonDrug: Education, self-management and continuation of normal activity as tolerated.
Exercise programme tailored to capability; include trunk/hip strength, mobility and graded aerobic activity.
Manual therapy only as part of a package including exercise.
Avoid routine traction, TENS, ultrasound and prolonged bed rest for non-specific LBP.
followUp: Early review if pain is severe or function is deteriorating; otherwise reassess response over the next few weeks.
Re-screen for red flags if symptoms change.
Persistent disabling symptoms: reassess diagnosis, psychosocial barriers and need for imaging/specialist opinion.

examination: Straight Leg Raise and Crossed SLR; document concordant radicular pain and side.
Slump test where appropriate.
Motor testing focused on L4/L5/S1, especially ankle dorsiflexion, great-toe extension and plantar flexion.
Dermatomal sensory mapping and patellar/Achilles reflexes.
Heel/toe walking and gait; quantify foot-drop weakness if present.
Screen cauda equina symptoms at every significant deterioration.

investigations.test: No routine plain X-ray for confirming disc herniation
investigations.indication: Disc herniation is a soft-tissue/neural diagnosis; X-ray does not show the herniated disc.
investigations.priority: Do not use as confirmatory test

investigations.test: X-ray Lumbosacral Spine — AP & Lateral views
investigations.indication: Use only for associated fracture/instability/bony structural concern, not simply because radicular pain is present.
Persistent/progressive radiculopathy, objective deficit, or when injection/surgery is being considered; document morphology and nerve-root concordance.
Suspected cauda equina syndrome or rapidly progressive major motor deficit.

medications.dose: 400 mg orally up to TID with food if NSAID appropriate.
medications.duration: Shortest appropriate course with early reassessment.
medications.notes: Use one NSAID only; screen GI/renal/CV/pregnancy/anticoagulant risks.

medications.dose: Typical total 75–150 mg/day divided; e.g. 50 mg BD if selected.
medications.notes: Alternative to ibuprofen, not in combination. Risk assessment and gastroprotection as appropriate.

nonDrug: Stay active within tolerance; avoid prolonged bed rest.
Graded rehabilitation with symptom-guided mobility and strengthening.
Selected acute severe radicular pain may be referred for epidural local anaesthetic + corticosteroid.
Surgical decompression/discectomy opinion when non-surgical care fails and imaging matches symptoms, or earlier for progressive neurological deficit.
followUp: Repeat motor examination and document any change in dorsiflexion/great-toe extension/plantar flexion.
Track pain/function plus neurological signs rather than MRI appearance alone.
Urgent referral for CES symptoms or progressive major weakness.

examination: Walking tolerance: distance/time to leg symptoms; document relief with sitting/flexion.
Compare standing/extension-provoked symptoms with sitting/flexion relief (shopping-cart phenotype).
Full lower-limb neurological exam: power, sensation, reflexes and gait.
Peripheral pulses and vascular examination to distinguish vascular claudication.
Hip examination for OA/hip mimic.
Assess balance and screen cervical/thoracic myelopathy if gait is disproportionate.

investigations.test: X-ray Lumbosacral Spine — standing AP & Lateral views
investigations.indication: Useful for alignment, degenerative spondylolisthesis, scoliosis and bony degeneration when structural assessment is needed.
Selected cases when dynamic instability/spondylolisthesis is suspected and the result would change management.
Preferred test to define central/lateral recess/foraminal stenosis when symptoms are clinically concordant and intervention is being considered.
If vascular claudication is a meaningful differential: diminished pulses, non-postural exertional symptoms or vascular risk profile.
New cauda equina symptoms or rapidly progressive neurological deficit.

medications.dose: 400 mg orally up to TID with/after food if clinically appropriate.
medications.duration: Shortest period; reassess symptom response and toxicity.
medications.notes: Symptom control only; does not reverse stenosis. Assess GI/renal/CV/pregnancy/anticoagulant risk.

medications.dose: 75–150 mg/day divided; e.g. 50 mg BD when selected.
medications.notes: Alternative NSAID only; avoid concurrent NSAIDs.

nonDrug: Education and flexion-tolerant/activity-based rehabilitation; progressive walking/cycling conditioning as tolerated.
Strength and balance programme individualized for age, frailty and neurological status.
Do not use epidural injections for neurogenic claudication due to central canal stenosis as routine treatment under NICE NG59.
Consider decompression opinion for persistent function-limiting neurogenic claudication with concordant imaging after appropriate non-surgical care.
followUp: Track walking distance/time, ODI or similar disability measure, neurological examination and falls risk.
Reassess vascular/hip differential if symptoms do not fit the postural neurogenic pattern.
Escalate immediately for CES or progressive motor deficit.

examination: Cervical active range of motion; note reproduction of arm symptoms.
Spurling test: reproduce concordant ipsilateral radicular arm pain with foraminal loading.
Upper Limb Tension Test (ULTT): useful as a sensitive neurodynamic test.
Shoulder abduction relief test where appropriate.
Motor examination by cervical myotomes (C5–T1), including deltoid, biceps, wrist extensors, triceps, finger flexors and hand intrinsics.
Sensory examination in root-related upper-limb distribution.
Reflexes: biceps C5-6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7.
Mandatory myelopathy screen: gait, hand dexterity, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann/clonus where indicated.

investigations.indication: Typical uncomplicated cervical radiculopathy without trauma/red flags and with a short symptom duration.

investigations.test: X-ray Cervical Spine — AP & Lateral ± oblique views
investigations.indication: Trauma, suspected bony/degenerative foraminal disease, malignancy red flag, or symptoms failing to improve after ~4–6 weeks. Oblique view can show bony foraminal narrowing.
Persistent symptoms after 4–6 weeks, progressive objective neurological deficit, suspected myelopathy, or when injection/surgery is considered.
When peripheral entrapment neuropathy or plexopathy is a significant competing diagnosis; not routinely required when clinical diagnosis is clear.
Myelopathy signs, rapidly progressive weakness, abscess/infection or other serious pathology.

medications.dose: 400 mg orally up to TID with food if an NSAID is appropriate.
medications.duration: Shortest appropriate period with early reassessment.
medications.notes: Symptomatic analgesic/anti-inflammatory option. Screen GI/renal/CV/pregnancy/anticoagulant risk; do not combine NSAIDs.

medications.dose: Typical adult total 75–150 mg/day in divided doses; e.g. 50 mg BD if clinically selected.
medications.notes: Alternative NSAID. Avoid duplicate NSAIDs; use individualized GI/CV/renal risk assessment.

nonDrug: Reassure that many cases improve with nonoperative care.
Physical therapy emphasizing cervical/shoulder/scapular strengthening and stretching.
Avoid forceful cervical manipulation if myelopathy, instability, fracture, infection or major neurological deficit is suspected.
Consider epidural/selective nerve-root intervention only after specialist review because of potential serious complications.
Spine referral if progressive deficit or persistent disabling symptoms with concordant imaging.
followUp: Repeat motor power, sensation and reflexes; progression of an objective neurological deficit should trigger MRI/referral.
Re-check gait, hand clumsiness and upper-motor-neuron signs for evolving myelopathy.
If not improving after 4–6 weeks, reassess diagnosis and imaging need.
